newsitem.title: IRAN: Conservatives criticise Iran president's cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives criticise Iran president's cabinet.

text.p: Conservative parliament members on Tuesday heavily criticised some of Iranian President Mohammad Khatami's cabinet choices and singled out his culture minister nominee as soft on a "Western cultural invasion".
Khatami, who was elected to parliament in May by a landslide, on Tuesday asked the conservative-led Majlis, or parliament, to approve all his 22 cabinet choices.
Minister designates must receive a vote of confidence from the 270-seat parliament to take office.
Seventeen deputies backed the moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric's cabinet choices during an initial five-hours session set aside for delegates urging support for a vote of confidence.

"In the elections people called for fundamental changes in the management of the country so as a deputy I feel obliged to respect the people's vote and agree with the proposed cabinet of the elected President," said deputy Lotfollah Zarei Qanavati.

But conservative deputies lashed out at some of the nominees -- particularly culture minister designate Ataollah Mohajerani and interior ministry nominee Abdollah Nouri -- during the day's second round of debate set aside for critics.

Abufazel Razavi Ardakani accused Mohajerani -- controversial for calling in 1990 for direct talks with Washington and his moderate views -- of being too "culturally tolerant and politically weak vis-a-vis the West".
"The main danger at this sensitive time is cultural leniency and liberalism and we promise...to resist it to the last drop of our blood," said deputy Ahmad Nejabat.

The Culture and Islamic Guidance Ministry has emerged as a battleground between Khatami's backers, who want to breathe more freedoms into the Islamic republic, and conservatives who see the body as a key weapon against a "Western cultural invasion".
It has a major influence on daily life as it decides what media, books, films and music are allowed in the country.
Conservatives and hardliners see Western cultural influences, especially among the youth, as a threat to the Islamic government.
Khatami was swept to power on expectations -- especially among the youth, women and the middle class -- that he would increase social and economic freedoms.
Khatami addressed the parliament before the cabinet debate, outlining his domestic agenda of a society "based on law" and an "active and fresh presence" in foreign affairs.
Razavi Ardakani criticised Nouri and cast doubt on his loyalty to the assembly and the country's supreme spiritual leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
"His track record shows he attaches no value to the Majlis. He isn't 100 percent obedient to the leadership," he said of Nouri.
Monireh Nobakht, a female deputy wearing a black chador, criticised Nouri for selecting regional governors on a purely political basis when he was interior minister from 1989 to 1993.
Khatami's cabinet nominees for agriculture, oil, higher education and transport also came under varying degrees of criticism.

Parliamentarian Davoud Danesh Jafari blasted Issa Kalantari, retained as agriculture minister by Khatami, accusing him of corruption and blaming him for Iran's increased dependence on imports of wheat and other foodstuffs.

On a more conciliatory note, influential conservative deputy Mohammad Reza Bahonar said: "Despite our principled criticism, we respect Mr Khatami's choices and will give our vote of confidence to most of the ministers, except for two or three."
The parliament is scheduled to vote on Wednesday after a third five-hour session during which cabinet nominees would defend themselves and their programmes.
